subtype: Approach: calming down before deciding what to do [Thinking]
passage:
Hemant: Zoya, you're still glaring at me. It was only a pen.
Zoya: Don't talk to me right now. My face is hot. If I speak, I'll say something mean.
Hemant: So what will you do?
Zoya: I'll read my book till lunch is over. Later, when I'm not shaking, I'll think about it properly.
Hemant: That's your whole plan?
Zoya: If I answer now it becomes a bigger fight. Later I can work out if I'm angry about the pen or about how you grabbed it.
Hemant: Fine. I'll be under the tree.
Zoya: Good. Not yet, Hemant.

qa.q: Where will Hemant wait while Zoya reads?
qa.a: Hemant will wait under the tree.

qa.q: What is Zoya feeling when Zoya's face turns hot?
qa.a: Zoya is angry and afraid of saying something mean, and wants to stay quiet until the feeling passes.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Zoya use later, and why?
qa.a: Zoya could tell Hemant calmly how the grabbing felt and ask what happened, since a calm talk lets both explain. Working out what actually happened is another way forward.

qa.q: How does Hemant see Zoya's silence?
qa.a: Hemant may find it hard to be told to wait, but agreeing to sit under the tree shows a willingness to give space instead of pushing.

grounding: After a fight over a borrowed pen, Zoya feels hot with anger and decides to stay quiet and think once calmer.

subtype: Approach: calming down before deciding what to do [Thinking]
passage: Last month my friend Madhav borrowed my new gel pen and gave it back with the tip squashed. He just laughed and said, 'It was already like that.' My face went so hot I could feel my ears. I had a whole speech ready, a mean one. But I knew if I opened my mouth then, I'd say something I couldn't take back. So I said nothing. At lunch I sat under the neem tree with my storybook instead of at our usual table. By the end of lunch my ears had cooled. I thought: Madhav probably pressed too hard, and maybe he was embarrassed. After school I said, 'Madhav, my pen broke. Can you be more careful?' He said sorry. Mummy said later, 'Simran beti, that was wise.'

qa.q: What did Madhav say about the pen?
qa.a: He laughed and said, 'It was already like that.'

qa.q: How did Simran feel when Madhav returned the squashed pen?
qa.a: Simran was so angry her face went hot and she could feel her ears, with a mean speech ready.

qa.q: What else could Simran do if she were still angry after lunch?
qa.a: Wait longer, or talk it over with a teacher or parent first; staying quiet while hot and speaking once calm is what kept the friendship.

qa.q: How might Madhav have experienced Simran's silence at lunch?
qa.a: Madhav may have noticed Simran sitting apart and felt uneasy, which could be why he said sorry after school.

grounding: Shows a girl who, hot with anger over a borrowed pen, stays silent, reads alone at lunch, and decides what to say once she is calm.

passage: Class teacher's note, Tuesday. Before lunch, Sabina and Sarita argued over a borrowed fountain pen: Sarita had kept it for two days and returned it leaking ink. Sabina's face went red and her hands were shaking. She didn't shout. She put the pen away, and at lunch she sat alone on the library steps with a book. I kept an eye on her from the staffroom window. After lunch she came to me and said, 'I was too angry to talk before. Now I can.' She and Sarita sorted it out at the water cooler in two minutes. I've told her I noticed the waiting.

qa.q: Where did Sabina sit at lunch?
qa.a: Alone on the library steps with a book.

qa.q: What do Sabina's red face and shaking hands suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: They suggest she was very angry about the leaking pen.
Waiting until she was calm, so when she spoke to Sarita it was sorted in two minutes instead of turning into a bigger fight.

qa.q: How might Sarita have seen Sabina's silence before lunch?
qa.a: Sarita might have felt uneasy, unsure whether Sabina was still upset, and relieved when they sorted it out at the water cooler.

grounding: Illustrates a girl who feels hot anger after a pen fight, says nothing, reads alone at lunch, and speaks only once she is calmer.
